description:
P0. Silent wrong answers from <, <=, >, >= on mixed int/float operands, on the NATIVE path only. Three-path parity violation. Blocks Enum.sort/max/min/sort_by and every numeric comparison a library function makes.

VERIFIED at 67e09d373, literals:
  expr                                    JIT              interp == Elixir
  {1 >= 1.0, 1.0 >= 1, 2 >= 1.0, 1 >= 2.0}  {f, t, f, f}     {t, t, t, f}
  {1 <= 1.0, 1.0 <= 1, 1 <= 2.0, 2 <= 1.0}  {t, f, t, t}     {t, t, t, f}
  {1 > 0.5,  1.0 > 1,  1 < 1.0}             {f, t, t}        {t, f, f}

8 of 11 wrong. '2 >= 1.0' returns false. '1 > 0.5' returns false.

NOT constant folding -- reproduces on values that arrive at runtime through a mailbox:
  i = 2 (int), f = 1.0 (float)
  {i >= f, f >= i, i > f, i == f}
    JIT             {false, true,  false, false}
    interp/Elixir   {true,  false, true,  false}

Every wrong result is explained by comparing the raw i64 against f64::to_bits() --
any float outranks any int, because 1.0 is 0x3FF0000000000000.

WHERE TO LOOK:
  - ir_interp/binop.rs:21 float_cmp! promotes BOTH sides via as_float -- correct.
  - native_codegen/prim.rs:1451 try_typed_binop_fast_path accepts only
    (RawInt,RawInt) | (RawF64,RawF64); mixed reprs return None.
  - prim.rs:1800+ the tagged fallback looks correct: it tests both_int on runtime
    tags and otherwise promotes via promote_f64 then fcmp.
  So the fast path is firing when it must not, or the operands reach it mis-reprd.
  Note ty_is_float/ty_is_int can BOTH be true for a union type such as
  'integer | float' -- then the float arm runs as_raw_f64 over an int-repr value,
  which is exactly a bit reinterpretation. Confirm before fixing.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE BUG (user, 2026-09-06). kernel.fz gives each ARITHMETIC operator
a four-clause typed family:
    fn left :: integer + right :: integer, do: fz_op_add_ii(left, right)
    fn left :: integer + right :: float,   do: fz_op_add_if(left, right)
    fn left :: float   + right :: integer, do: fz_op_add_if(right, left)
    fn left :: float   + right :: float,   do: fz_op_add_ff(left, right)
and prim.rs:1474 documents lower_arith_binop as having an explicit
'float coercion (int+float mix)' path. Every COMPARISON operator has exactly one
untyped clause instead:
    @spec any < any :: bool
    fn left < right, do: fz_op_lt(left, right)

FIX: give <, <=, >, >=, ==, != the same typed clause families the arithmetic
operators already have, so each mixed case is routed to a correctly-typed extern by
construction instead of relying on an any-typed lowering to sort it out at runtime.
That also fixes fz-5xp.9 (1 == 1.0 is false) in the same motion -- == and != need
the integer/float and float/integer clauses to compare numerically.

Keep the any-typed clause as the fallback for non-numeric operands; it stays the seat
that fz-5xp.8 (term ordering) will fill.

GATE: an oracle fixture covering the full mixed-comparison cross product on all three
paths. No fixture compares mixed int/float today, which is why this survived.

comments.text:
Design revised after measurement (user, 2026-09-07).

VERIFIED ROOT SHAPE. Equality and ordering are built differently, and that is the bug class:
  equality  interp interp_value_eq -> fz_value_eq_ref   native calls fz_value_eq_ref   ONE shared fn, doors agree
  ordering  interp its own float_cmp! macro             native its own both_int/brif/box/promote   TWO impls, doors diverged
fz_value_eq_ref exists (runtime/src/ir_runtime.rs:2032); there is no fz_value_cmp counterpart. Ordering is the outlier.

PLAN.
  1. kernel.fz gives each of < <= > >= == != the four typed numeric clauses (ii, if, fi, ff) plus an any/any default, mirroring the arithmetic operators.
  2. The typed clauses lower to inline comparisons on raw lanes: same-kind through the existing typed fast path, mixed through fcvt_from_sint + fcmp (new, prim.rs lower_mixed_numeric_cmp).
  3. The any/any default calls a REAL runtime function for ordering, shaped like fz_value_eq_ref, called by BOTH doors.
  4. DELETE lower_cmp_binop's fallback (both_int test, brif, box_float_for_any, fz_promote_f64 pair). It is what boxed a raw f64 and then read the pointer as a number.
  5. fz-5xp.8 then implements Erlang term order in that one function instead of two.

MEASURED ALONG THE WAY (do not re-derive):
  - Three clauses (if/fi/any) fix mixed ordering on both doors but do NOT make the codegen fallback dead: the any/any body still correctly serves dynamic int/int and dynamic float/float, both verified against Elixir. Only the five-clause form makes it dead.
  - == and != with clauses cost a real dispatch. Verified mechanism: NOT 'dispatch inside a guard' -- a homogeneous '2 in [1,2,3]' keeps 0 call-edge dispatches through the same when-head==value guard. The cause is a shared generic member? activation whose operands are a union (integer from list/range, tuple from map), so a multi-clause == has more than one candidate target there. membership_operator.fz goes 0 -> 3 call-edge dispatches.
  - compiler2_membership_operator_protocol_receivers_settle_to_direct_impls is misnamed for what it asserts: it scans EVERY executable for any DirectCall whose target is a CallEdge::Dispatch, not protocol receivers specifically (drive_test.rs:12196). Nothing about protocol settling regressed.
  - Operators are ALREADY out-of-line today: fz_op_gte__e9 is its own executable with a call in the single-clause build. Clauses add selection, not a new call.
  - Cost of the three-clause ordering form: work applies 4104 -> 4144, evaluations 989 -> 1049, entry plans 156 -> 157.

Inlining these one-expression operator bodies would remove a call that exists today, for every operator, independent of this ticket -- filed separately.

title: Native mixed int/float comparison is wrong; interpreter is right
